- **LANDED (chunk #77 — 2026-05-22):** Drain LogHub-style golden corpus regression harness (audit Section 3.S — algorithm correctness verified via unit tests but no golden directory visible pre-chunk-#77):
  - **[LANDED chunk #77]** `drain-golden-corpus-coverage: regression harness` — committed LogHub-style log line fixtures + expected Drain template extraction output; regression test asserts Drain mining output matches golden against synthetic 50-100 line fixtures covering 3-5 template shapes (NUM masking + IPv4 masking + email masking per chunk #69 e2e_drain_template_assignment.rs precedent). Materialized at `crates/buffer/tests/drain_golden_corpus.rs` with fixtures at `crates/buffer/tests/fixtures/drain/`.

- **Boot smoke check gap** (chunks touching boot/setup paths lack runtime smoke gating; chunk #27/#30 latent panic at `crates/ui-bridge/src/health.rs:291` "there is no reactor running, must be called from the context of a Tokio 1.x runtime" went undetected through 4 wrap cycles before chunk #31's Phase 2b smoke gate caught it):
  - `boot-smoke-coverage: per-chunk Tauri dev smoke gate` — chunks touching `pulse-app/src/main.rs`, `pulse-app/src/engine_boot.rs` (since chunk 2026-10-10-console-engine-entry-point the process start `init_process` and the whole engine composition `start`, which both programs boot through, moved out of `main.rs`), `crates/ui-bridge/src/`, `pulse-app/src/observability.rs` (boot-time subscriber/allowlist init, before the OTLP bind), `pulse-app/src-tauri/tauri.conf.json`, OR `pulse-app/capabilities/*.json` MUST include `npx @tauri-apps/cli dev` (60s timeout; boot-completion signal detection: `Local:` / `ready in` / `Compiled successfully` from stdout) in their `## Test Commands` section. Where the verification needs runtime state that form cannot express (a fresh `ANDROMEDA_PULSE_DATA_DIR`, an env-gated mode, a sustained `inject_demo` load), the direct-binary smoke variant is the accepted alternative — see test-plan §3 "Direct-binary smoke variant" (the harness `boot` verb is that form over `target/release/pulse-app`; `boot engine`, sh only, is the same form over `target/release/andromeda-pulse-engine run`). The window smoke boots `pulse-app` alone: a chunk touching `pulse-app/src/console.rs` or `pulse-app/src/bin/andromeda-pulse-engine.rs` takes the spawned-program test `pulse-app/tests/integration_console_engine.rs` as its runtime gate (test-plan §3 "Spawned-program witness form"), and one whole run of the console engine under the harness is read by `cargo xtask harness:engine-cycle` (test-plan §3 "Engine cycle gate form"). Smoke check classification per `andromeda-implement/references/runtime-failure-patterns.md` (capability-drift → /andromeda-scope-arch; Tauri capability JSON → /andromeda-arch; schema_version mismatch → /andromeda-wrap-session; etc.). On Phase 2b smoke failure, chunk surfaces "green per scope; runtime blocked by out-of-scope issue(s)" variant per /andromeda-implement Phase 3 — chunk implementation commits as-is; runtime blocker addressed via the suggested redirect skill OR follow-up chunk.
  - Per amendment `2026-05-09T16-00-54Z-smoke-check-boot-discipline` (`.andromeda/runs/2026-05-09T16-00-54-spec-amendment-smoke-check-boot-discipline/amendment.md`).

- **Chunk-plan standard-gate baseline gap** (chunks #35-#36 committed with pre-existing fmt + tsc failures because their plan gate lists were incomplete; chunk #37's plan included the full set and exposed the inherited failures):
  - `chunk-gate-baseline-coverage: standard gate set unconditional per chunk` — every `/andromeda-phase`-authored chunk plan's `## Test Commands` section MUST list the FULL standard gate set: `cargo fmt --check` + `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings` + `cargo xtask capability-widening-check` + `cargo xtask check:ingest-progress` + `cargo xtask check:staged-artifacts` (staged git-index bindings + capability grants vs `EXPECTED_PROCEDURES` / `staged_gate::EXPECTED_GRANTS`; exit 0/1/2) + `cargo xtask capability-drift` (BEFORE the default-features workspace nextest, which rewrites `bindings/index.ts` in the default build's shape, the whole procedure set, so it does not shrink the bindings — overseer directive 2026-09-30; since 2026-08-30-staged-bindings-assertion the staged assertion is CODE folded into this gate itself, superseding playbook 2026-08-22's interim manual staged-copy check) + `cargo nextest run --workspace --profile ci` + the no-feature `emit_taurpc_bindings` regen (the last cargo-adjacent step) + `git diff --quiet <chunk-base> -- pulse-app/ui/src/bindings/index.ts` (the close, for a chunk adding no procedure; a chunk that CHANGES the procedure set closes instead with a content probe on the regenerated worktree bindings (the new procedure's name) → `git add` of the bindings WITH the `EXPECTED_PROCEDURES` pin → `check:staged-artifacts`, then `capability-drift` LAST, and runs the regen BEFORE the `ui/dist` build and every release build a live leg drives — test-plan §3, measured 2026-09-30) + (when chunk's `Files-to-modify`/`New-files-to-create` lists touch any `pulse-app/ui/**` paths) `npm run lint --prefix pulse-app/ui` + `npm run typecheck --prefix pulse-app/ui` + `npm run test --prefix pulse-app/ui`. Webview gates excluded only when chunk touches zero `pulse-app/ui/**` paths. A plan that lists a build-branch push lists the merge-base probe directly before it, on the operator leg (`m="$(git ls-remote origin refs/heads/main | cut -f1)" && test -n "$m" && git merge-base --is-ancestor "$m" HEAD`, `expect = ['exit 0']`): red when the build branch does not contain the remote's `main` as it stands then, brought to the operator before any push — the pull-request run builds the tip merged with `main`, the local pre-push check the tip alone (test-plan §3 Per-chunk gate discipline, since 2026-10-10). Boot-smoke conditional per existing `boot-smoke-coverage` trigger (cumulative, not exclusive). Without the unconditional baseline, gate-coverage drift accumulates as carry-overs that surface only when a downstream chunk's broader gate list catches them — effectively delaying detection by N chunks. Pre-flight gate parity at chunk-plan authoring time prevents this gap.
  - Per amendment `2026-05-10T12-41-03Z-mandate-standard-chunk-gates` (`.andromeda/runs/2026-05-10T12-41-03-spec-amendment-mandate-standard-chunk-gates/amendment.md`).

- **RETIRED 2026-08-26 — Living-artifact tooling re-run discipline** (its subject no longer exists):
  - `living-artifact-tooling-rerun-coverage` — RETIRED, kept for the audit trail. It required wrap-session Phase 5 to run the Tooling command from each `.andromeda/context/{artifact}.md` METADATA at every wrap (skip-on-webview-only forbidden). Both living-doc artifacts (`.andromeda/context/api-surface.md`, `dependency-tree.md`) were deleted at commit `5a83771` (2026-06-28) and no `context/` directory exists; the code-graph (`.andromeda/cache/{plane}/tree.db`, derived, gitignored, rebuilt on demand by /andromeda-phase and /andromeda-wrap-session) replaced them and has no LIVING block to reconcile (test-plan §1 Pending coverage triggers).
  - Per amendment `2026-05-10T12-41-03Z-mandate-living-artifact-tooling-rerun` (`.andromeda/runs/2026-05-10T12-41-03-spec-amendment-mandate-living-artifact-tooling-rerun/amendment.md`).
- **Single crate:** `cargo nextest run --filter-expr 'package(ingest)'`
- **All workspace:** `cargo nextest run --workspace --profile ci --message-format libtest-json`
- **With coverage:** `cargo llvm-cov nextest --workspace --lcov --output-path lcov.info --summary-only`
- **xtask shortcut:** `cargo xtask test`

- **Release/tag gates (chunk #99):** `cargo xtask verify:capability-matrix` (the capability record's gate, P-001–P-082 each claimed or retired; also a per-PR CI step) + `cargo xtask perf:load-profiles` (four-profile suite, then the in-process `xtask::perf_budget` grader with no arm required, printing `perf:load-profiles: perf-budget {verdict}` — release/tag cadence, not per-PR).

- **CI runners:** `ubuntu-22.04` alone — five jobs (lint-test · a11y · boot · supply-chain · coverage), no matrix (since chunk 2026-10-09-ci-on-linux-alone; pinned by `ci_workflow_runs_on_linux_only`). The E2E `webview-drive` leg is wired into no workflow.
_This section is owned by `/wrap-session`. setup-project preserves content added here on re-run._

- 2026-05-03: `#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]` requires the `test-util` feature on the `tokio` workspace dep — the workspace currently pins `features = ["full"]`, which does NOT include `test-util` (per tokio docs the `full` feature unifies fs/io/macros/net/process/rt/sync/time/tracing but excludes test-util). Compile fails with `no method named 'start_paused' found for struct 'tokio::runtime::Builder'` — misleading because the missing capability is a feature gate, not a missing method. Two paths: (a) drop `start_paused = true` from tests that don't actually need paused clock (smoke tests / spawn-and-abort tests run fine on real time within milliseconds); (b) add `tokio = { workspace = true, features = ["test-util"] }` to the affected crate's `[dev-dependencies]` to unify in test builds without bloating production. Default to (a) when the test doesn't assert on tick cadence — keeps dev-dep surface minimal. Use (b) only when the test genuinely needs `tokio::time::pause()` + `tokio::time::advance(Duration)` semantics (e.g., retention-window tests; multi-interval timing assertions).

- 2026-05-04: motion v12's `useReducedMotion` hook from `motion/react` (verified 12.38.0) is intentionally NON-reactive after mount: the hook captures `prefersReducedMotion.current` via `useState(...)` on mount and never re-renders on subsequent media-query change (per framer-motion source TODO comment in `node_modules/framer-motion/dist/es/utils/reduced-motion/use-reduced-motion.mjs`). The matchMedia listener is single-global, registered ONCE per process via motion-dom's `initPrefersReducedMotion()` lazy-init on first hook call; subsequent hook mounts read the cached ref. Test consequence for Vitest specs consuming `useReducedMotion`: MUST reset motion-dom's module-global state between tests via `import { hasReducedMotionListener, prefersReducedMotion } from "motion-dom"; hasReducedMotionListener.current = false; prefersReducedMotion.current = null;` in `beforeEach`. Without the reset, the FIRST test's `mockReducedMotion(value)` is captured globally and subsequent tests with different values get the stale prior state. Per-instance `addEventListener` / `removeEventListener` spies are NOT a valid contract — assert global subscription pattern instead (matchMedia called once + addEventListener called once globally on first hook mount). The older "reactive on every change" framer-motion behavior is NOT preserved in motion v12. See `pulse-app/ui/src/hooks/use-reduced-motion.test.tsx` for canonical pattern.

- 2026-05-05: When integration tests boot a server that takes a `tokio::sync::mpsc::Sender` (or wrapper around one), the test MUST hold the matching `Receiver` alive for the test duration — either by returning it from the helper tuple OR by spawning a placeholder consumer task `tokio::spawn(async move { while receiver.recv().await.is_some() {} })` that drains messages. Dropping the receiver before the test completes causes `Sender::try_send` to return `TrySendError::Closed` immediately on subsequent calls, and the receiver-side endpoints fail with the channel-saturated error path (HTTP 503 / gRPC `ResourceExhausted`) instead of the expected success path. The chunk #18 helpers `crates/ingest/tests/{grpc_loopback,http_loopback}.rs::start_test_*_server` show both patterns: `grpc_loopback.rs` uses the spawn-drainer pattern (no receiver returned); `tests/invariants.rs::start_test_grpc_server` uses the return-tuple pattern (receiver returned to the test for explicit `rx.recv().await` assertions verifying the batch landed in the channel). Choose return-tuple when the test asserts on channel content; choose spawn-drainer when the test only cares about the response code. Both are valid; ad-hoc ignoring the receiver is not.

- 2026-05-06: `#[tokio::test(start_paused = true)]` is INCOMPATIBLE with `flavor = "multi_thread"` — only `flavor = "current_thread"` (the default) supports paused clock semantics. Compile error is explicit: `error: The 'start_paused' option requires the 'current_thread' runtime flavor. Use #[tokio::test(flavor = "current_thread")]`. This rules out the common chunk #20 pattern `#[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 4)]` for any test that also needs `tokio::time::pause()` clock injection. Resolution: drop the `multi_thread` flavor + `worker_threads` for paused-clock tests (chunk #21 retention.rs initial design hit this); use `flavor = "current_thread"` and structure the test to NOT depend on multi-threaded scheduling. If a test genuinely needs both (rare — usually means the test is asserting too much about runtime internals), refactor to extract a sync/async helper from the periodic loop body and test the helper directly without paused-clock orchestration. See `crates/buffer/src/retention.rs::run_one_sweep` extraction for the canonical "extract testable async helper" pattern that sidestepped the start_paused × multi_thread × spawn_blocking × abort race entirely.

- 2026-05-07: To verify `tracing::warn!` / `tracing::error!` event emission in unit tests WITHOUT adding the `tracing-test` crate to workspace deps, implement a minimal `tracing::Subscriber` (~25 lines) capturing `(target, level)` tuples into a thread-shared `Arc<Mutex<Vec<(String, tracing::Level)>>>` via the trait's `event()` callback (other required methods — `enabled` / `new_span` / `record` / `record_follows_from` / `enter` / `exit` — can be no-op stubs). Drive it through `tracing::subscriber::with_default(subscriber, closure)` which scopes the subscriber to the current thread for the closure's duration; tests don't pollute each other across nextest's per-process isolation. Assertion shape: `assert!(events.iter().any(|(target, level)| target == "X" && *level == tracing::Level::WARN))`. Trade-off vs the `tracing-test` crate's `#[traced_test]` macro: the in-process pattern needs no extra workspace dep + no per-crate dev-dep, but lacks the macro's `logs_contain(...)` / fields-level assertion ergonomics. Choose in-process when (a) workspace dep budget is tight, OR (b) the verification only needs "event emitted at target X with level ≥ WARN" (no field content). For chunk #26's `From<E> for AppError` tests, the in-process pattern was chosen — see `crates/ui-bridge/src/contract.rs::tests::CapturingSubscriber` + `capture()` helper. Pairs naturally with rstest fixtures for parametric From-impl coverage.

- 2026-05-08: Vitest tests asserting the call count of useEffect-driven mocks in React 19 components must use `toHaveBeenCalled()` (≥1 call) rather than `toHaveBeenCalledTimes(N)` (exact count). Empirically observed in chunk #28's `pulse-app/ui/src/canvas/CanvasContainer.test.tsx`: an effect creating 3 render-pipeline factories ran twice during a single mount despite no StrictMode wrapper; both mockClear() in `afterEach` AND fresh stubGpuAvailable() per test confirmed this is per-test, not cross-test bleed. Likely cause is React 19 dev-mode useEffect double-invocation (analogous to React 18 StrictMode behavior) interacting with the `[adapter, reducedMotion]` dependency change as the async adapter resolution settles. Resolution: relax assertions to "was called" semantics for any factory invoked from a useEffect that depends on async-resolved state. Strict counts work for effects with stable refs from mount only (no async deps); strict counts fail for effects whose dependency array transitions between renders. Documenting because this trap will recur for every Epoch 5 surface that consumes the canvas substrate via async adapter resolution.

- 2026-05-08: Vitest's `vi.stubGlobal('navigator', {...})` and similar global stubs are NOT auto-restored between tests — `pulse-app/ui/src/test-setup.ts` global `afterEach(cleanup)` only invokes `@testing-library/react` cleanup (DOM unmount), it does not reset Vitest globals. Tests that stub `navigator.gpu`, `navigator.userAgent`, `localStorage`, etc. MUST explicitly call `vi.unstubAllGlobals()` in their own per-test-file `afterEach` block, OR the prior test's stub leaks into subsequent tests in the same file (and across files if Vitest's per-file isolation is relaxed via `--no-isolate`). Verified in chunk #28's `webgpu-adapter.test.ts` and `CanvasContainer.test.tsx` where leaked `navigator.gpu = undefined` from one test caused a later "available" path test to incorrectly hit the unavailable branch. Pattern landed in both files: `afterEach(() => { vi.unstubAllGlobals(); })`. Note: prototype mutations (e.g., `HTMLCanvasElement.prototype.getContext = vi.fn()...`) ALSO are not auto-restored — manual restoration or `vi.spyOn(HTMLCanvasElement.prototype, 'getContext')` (which is auto-restored) is the safer pattern for those.

- 2026-05-09: For unit tests asserting `tracing::info!` / `tracing::warn!` event emission inside an `#[tokio::test]` async resolver, use `tracing::subscriber::set_default(subscriber)` (returns a `DefaultGuard` scoped to the current thread until dropped) — NOT the 2026-05-07 `tracing::subscriber::with_default(subscriber, closure)` pattern. `with_default` takes a SYNC closure; trying to drive an async future via `tokio::runtime::Builder::new_current_thread().build().block_on(future)` inside the closure fails with `Cannot start a runtime from within a runtime` because `#[tokio::test]` already established a current_thread runtime context. The `set_default` guard pattern works because guards scope thread-locally and the `.await` polls within the same thread between `set_default` (acquire) and `drop(guard)` (release). Test shape: `let guard = tracing::subscriber::set_default(subscriber); api.method(input).await.expect("ok"); drop(guard); let captured = events.lock().expect("lock").clone();`. Pattern used in `crates/ui-bridge/src/telemetry.rs::tests::record_frame_ms_emits_tracing_info_at_metric_target_on_success` (chunk #29). Pairs with the 2026-05-07 in-process `CapturingSubscriber` impl — same Subscriber implementation, different scoping primitive depending on sync vs async test body.

- 2026-05-09: jsdom does not expose runtime WebGPU constants (`GPUBufferUsage`, `GPUTextureUsage`, etc.); `vi.stubGlobal("GPUBufferUsage", { UNIFORM: 0x40, COPY_DST: 0x08, ... })` proved UNRELIABLE across test ordering at chunk #31. Empirically: 5 of 8 HaloCanvas tests passed with the stub, but the FIRST 3 tests in the file failed with `ReferenceError: GPUBufferUsage is not defined` despite identical setup pattern (stubGpuAvailable() called at top of each test, including the GPUBufferUsage stub). Root cause unconfirmed (possibly a getter/setter property descriptor interaction with jsdom's window or React 19 dev-mode useEffect double-flush timing relative to vi.unstubAllGlobals in afterEach). The reliable fix is to inline the WebGPU spec constant value as a module-level numeric literal in the production code itself: `const UNIFORM_BUFFER_USAGE = 0x40 | 0x08; // GPUBufferUsage.UNIFORM | GPUBufferUsage.COPY_DST per WebGPU spec`. Production WebGPU runtime exposes the same constant values per spec (https://www.w3.org/TR/webgpu/#typedefdef-gpubufferusageflags), so the inline form is portable + sidesteps the jsdom test fragility entirely. Pattern landed in `pulse-app/ui/src/halo/HaloCanvas.tsx::UNIFORM_BUFFER_USAGE`. Apply to any future webview component that calls `device.createBuffer({ usage: ... })` or other WebGPU APIs that take spec-constant flag bitfields. Pairs naturally with the 2026-05-08 `vi.unstubAllGlobals` discipline (which is still required for `navigator` + `userAgent` stubs, just not viable for the runtime-WebGPU-constant globals).

- 2026-05-09: Adding `npx @tauri-apps/cli dev` (or equivalent runtime smoke) to a chunk's Test Commands gates against latent boot panics that compile + unit tests + lint never catch. Chunks #27-#30 introduced new TauRPC routers (chunk #27 IntrospectionApi at `crates/ui-bridge/src/health.rs:291` `#[taurpc::procedures]`) + boot helpers (chunk #30 `Settings::load_from_data_dir` + `apply_widget_settings`) without including a runtime smoke in their gate list — chunk #30 committed (19bfbf2) green per its scope but ships a latent panic at boot: `panic_message: "there is no reactor running, must be called from the context of a Tokio 1.x runtime"` at `crates/ui-bridge/src/health.rs:291`. Chunk #31 added Phase 2b smoke via /andromeda-implement and surfaced the panic — but as out-of-scope for chunk #31 (no Rust changes touched). Future chunk plans whose `## Test Commands` section touches `pulse-app/src/main.rs`, `crates/ui-bridge/src/`, or any other boot/setup path SHOULD include `npx @tauri-apps/cli dev` (60s timeout, watch for `Local:` / `ready in` / `Compiled successfully`) so latent panics are caught at the introducing chunk's gate rather than surfacing several chunks later. Smoke check status (success / failure / skipped-headless / skipped-no-cli) belongs in plan acceptance criteria, not just in Test Commands, to surface clearly in commit message body. **[extended 2026-08-22]** And the CHUNK PLAN's own claim about whether this gate applies can be FALSE — verify against the trigger path list itself, never the plan's prose. At 2026-08-22-pii-scrubber-recall the plan's Test Commands asserted "none of this chunk's paths are on the boot-smoke trigger list" while the chunk modified `pulse-app/src/observability.rs`, which that list names literally; running the smoke anyway was load-bearing (it produced the only wire-level proof the new counter reaches the log unredacted). The plan is a proposal about the gate, not the gate's definition.

- 2026-05-09: Tauri 2 webview API modules (`@tauri-apps/api/webviewWindow`, `@tauri-apps/api/window`, `@tauri-apps/api/event`) import successfully in jsdom but throw at call time when `window.__TAURI_INTERNALS__` is undefined. Pattern for testing chunks that consume Tauri runtime APIs: `vi.mock("@tauri-apps/api/webviewWindow", () => ({ getCurrentWebviewWindow: vi.fn() }))` at top of test file (vi.mock hoists before the actual import), then per-test `vi.mocked(getCurrentWebviewWindow).mockReturnValue({ label: "compact-widget" } as ReturnType<typeof getCurrentWebviewWindow>)` with type-cast escape (the full WebviewWindow type has 30+ members; tests only need .label). Combine with `vi.mocked(...).mockReset()` in `afterEach` so tests don't leak stub state across describe blocks. - 2026-05-14: High-volume span fixtures for load tests MUST generate globally-unique `(trace_id, span_id)` pairs per span — the buffer schema's composite primary key silently drops duplicates at the DuckDB Arrow appender step, so duplicate-key spans don't surface as a panic or error; they just don't increment `BufferState::rows_ingested`. The chunk #50 P1 pattern `(i % 250) + 1` byte for span_id is fine for 100 spans (no collisions) but cycles after 250 spans → at 100k-span load, only ~250 spans land + the test asserts rows_ingested == 0 after 12s timeout. Fix pattern: encode batch_idx LE-bytes into trace_id (e.g., `unique_trace_id(batch_seed) -> [batch_seed.to_le_bytes() ++ [1; 8]]`) AND encode batch_seed × BATCH_SIZE + span_idx into 8-byte span_id (`unique_span_id(batch_seed, span_idx) -> ((batch_seed * BATCH_SIZE + span_idx + 1).to_le_bytes())`). Verified at chunk #54 `pulse-app/tests/perf_slo_10k_spans.rs` after initial implementation produced rows_ingested = 0 / panicked at 12s timeout. Generalizes to any future load test or chaos test injecting >250 spans (chunk #56 obs CI gate perf-budget regression detection will reuse this generator shape; future tauri-driver headful tests injecting volume-bound load will also need it). The buffer schema's PK structure is documented in arch §Conventions Primary key convention; the fixture-generator implication is what was non-obvious until empirically observed. Apply pre-emptively: any fixture generator emitting >250 spans MUST use a monotonic counter encoded into ≥3 bytes of span_id, not a modulo cycle. **2026-08-16 EXTENSION — the drop is not merely a lost row: the fingerprint observer sits DOWNSTREAM of the append gate, so a span rejected for a colliding `(trace_id, span_id)` never reaches storm detection at all.** A producer that reuses ids therefore yields an UNDETECTABLE storm: the detector's counters stay flat and read exactly like a dead feed, making an id collision indistinguishable from a broken pipeline. Measured in BOTH directions on live external-harness legs against this repo's HEAD — a colliding producer detected nothing; the same producer with unique ids detected the storm. Discipline for any harness or test driving storm detection: assert `rows_ingested` actually advanced BEFORE concluding anything from a zero detector count, otherwise a fixture defect will be diagnosed as a product regression.

- 2026-05-14: Test mocks of overloaded DOM methods (`vi.spyOn(Prototype, "method").mockImplementation(() => ({...}) as unknown as <SpecificType>)`) break when `@types/web` (or any DOM types package) expands the method's return overload union after the test was written. Verified at chunk #53 wrap when `pulse-app/ui/src/dashboard/routes/metrics/MetricsChart.test.tsx` (chunk #35-era; 2026-05-10) emitted TS2739 "Type 'CanvasRenderingContext2D' is missing the following properties from type 'GPUCanvasContext': __brand, configure, unconfigure, getConfiguration, getCurrentTexture" during chunk #53's full standard-gate baseline run — the narrow `as unknown as CanvasRenderingContext2D` cast satisfied only the 2d overload return; the webgpu overload added to the `getContext` union in a later @types/web release broke the narrowing. Fix: replace the narrow cast with `as never`. `never` is the bottom type, assignable to every overload return shape; the mock function accepts arbitrary overload conformances. Trade-off: loses the static-type assertion that the mock IS a specific context type, but test bodies inspect the mock by selected method calls (e.g. `expect(clearRect).toHaveBeenCalled()`), not by static type — so the loss is purely cosmetic. Complementary to the 2026-05-10 jsdom-getContext-null-stub pattern (stubbing IS still correct; the type-cast inside the stub is what needs updating when DOM types evolve). Applies to any future test mocking overloaded DOM methods (`getContext` / `addEventListener` / `postMessage` / etc.) — pre-emptively prefer `as never` over a narrow cast at the moment of writing the mock, OR migrate existing narrow casts to `as never` when type expansion breaks them. Side note: this drift surfaced via chunk-gate-baseline-coverage (chunks touching zero `pulse-app/ui/**` still run webview gates per the trigger) — the unconditional gate set is a secondary defense against latent test-fixture drift in untouched files.

env:
")` looking for a top-level YAML key fails to match on Windows even though the key IS present — because the byte sequence between `env:` and the next line is `
` not `

Fix pattern: `let lines: Vec<&str> = content.lines().collect(); let idx = lines.iter().position(|line| *line == "env:").expect(...);` — `str::lines()` per the std docs strips BOTH `

- 2026-06-05 (session 178): BACKGROUND command exit code masked by `| tail`/`| head`/`| grep`. When a long build/test is launched via the Bash tool with `run_in_background: true`, piping it to `tail`/`head`/`grep` makes the PIPELINE's exit code = the filter's exit code (tail almost always exits 0), so the completion `<task-notification>` reports "exit code 0" even when the wrapped command actually FAILED. Verified this session: `cargo nextest run --workspace --profile ci 2>&1 | tail -30` run in background was reported "completed (exit code 0)" while cargo had in fact exited 101 (cold-build-race rlib errors per the 2026-05-31 session-165 entry) — the real failure was visible ONLY by reading the captured output file. Discipline for backgrounded long builds/tests (common here due to ~20-30 min cold rebuilds after `cargo clean`): run the command RAW (no trailing `| tail`), e.g. `cargo build --workspace && cargo nextest run --workspace --profile ci`, so the true exit code propagates to the task-notification; then `tail`/`grep` the background OUTPUT FILE (path returned in the launch result) for the summary. A `&&` chain's exit code correctly reflects the first failing stage; a `| tail` pipeline's does not (set `pipefail` is not in effect for the tool's default shell wrapper, and even with it `tail` masking is fragile). Foreground commands are unaffected (output is inline + you see cargo's own error). Pairs with the 2026-05-31 session-165 cold-build-race entry: that one de-races the build (`cargo build --workspace`/`-p pulse-app` before nextest); this one ensures you actually SEE whether the de-raced background build succeeded instead of trusting a tail-masked exit 0. **[extended 2026-08-28] The same truncation also poisons a WAIT PREDICATE, and there it fails LOUDER but less visibly.** Having correctly run the command raw, a follow-up `until grep -qE '<pattern>' <output-file>; do sleep N; done` can key on a line the command's OWN `| tail -8` had already discarded — so the pattern never appears, the loop never exits, and it keeps spinning long after the work finished; the user sees unexplained shell activity rather than a wrong result. Measured this session: a gate chain piped through `tail -8` dropped nextest's `Summary [` line, and the wait-loop polling for it survived its own 600 s ceiling and had to be killed by task id. **Rule: a wait predicate must key on the task's COMPLETION (the background task id / its exit), never on a string in a log the producer may have truncated** — and if you must grep, grep for something the producer cannot drop (a marker your own wrapper writes), not for a tool's summary line. **[extended 2026-08-30] Under `set -o pipefail`, `producer | grep -q` INVERTS on match** — `grep -q` exits at the FIRST match, the producer takes SIGPIPE and dies non-zero, and pipefail propagates that, so the pipeline FAILS exactly when the pattern is FOUND; a poll loop keyed on "pipeline success = found" then never advances on a healthy run (measured at the 2026-08-30 sweep smoke: the phase poll sat inert and degraded to a fixed wait; the evidence reads were unaffected because post-hoc `grep -c` reads a file, not a pipe). In a pipefail script, test for a pattern with `grep -c` (reads to EOF) or grep a FILE, never `producer | grep -q`. - 2026-06-28: A thread-local `tracing::subscriber::set_default` does NOT reliably capture a resolver's tracing events emitted AFTER an internal `tokio::task::spawn_blocking`, when the test runs under in-process PARALLEL libtest (`cargo test`). Mechanism: `cargo test` runs test fns on parallel threads; the `spawn_blocking` continuation can resume on a thread WITHOUT the thread-local `set_default` subscriber, so the post-spawn_blocking emit (e.g. a resolver's `tracing::info!` after a blocking DuckDB load) lands where no subscriber sees it → captured events = `[]`. `cargo nextest`'s per-process isolation is UNAFFECTED (one test per process), so the same test passes under nextest but FAILS under `cargo test` — a runner-dependent flake (the workspace gate is nextest, but don't ship a runner-dependent test). EXTENDS the 2026-05-07 / 2026-05-09 `set_default`-for-async-test entries — those hold for async tests WITHOUT a `spawn_blocking` thread-hop; this is the case they don't cover. Fix: when a test must capture a resolver's post-`spawn_blocking` obs AND pass under both runners, install the subscriber via `tracing::subscriber::set_global_default(subscriber)` (process-global → captures across ALL threads incl. the spawn_blocking continuation) — safe when the test is the ONLY subscriber-setter in that integration-test binary (one call per process; nextest gives each test its own process, libtest calls it once). AND assert the SPECIFIC target event IS captured (`captured.iter().any(|(t, _)| t == "investigate.run_action.request")`), never just `!captured.is_empty()` — otherwise a PII / no-leak loop over `captured` passes VACUOUSLY on an empty capture (the silent-vacuous-test trap; caught this session when the canary loop "passed" against zero captured events). Verified at chunk 2026-06-28-investigate-actions-functional `pulse-app/tests/integration_investigate_actions.rs::investigate_does_not_log_telemetry_canary`. **[extended 2026-08-27 — a SECOND mechanism produces the same runner-dependent empty capture, with NO `spawn_blocking` involved.]** A thread-local `with_default` capture can come back missing the asserted event when SIBLING tests in the same binary exercise the SAME `tracing::` callsites in parallel with no subscriber installed — the callsite interest cache races the thread-local dispatcher, and the more no-subscriber siblings the binary gains, the likelier the flake (measured at `2026-08-26-interpretation-brief-completeness`: `producer_observability_is_aggregate_only` failed under parallel `cargo test` only after the chunk added 4 sibling tests calling `create_incident_from_l4_output`; solo-run and nextest always green). Same fix (`set_global_default`, sole-setter binary) — plus the corollary the first case didn't need: a process-GLOBAL subscriber also captures the SIBLINGS' events under libtest, so find-first assertions get poisoned by a sibling's same-target record — assert with `any` over the FULL field signature (`t == target && fields.contains(a) && fields.contains(b)…`), and keep canary strings unique to the asserting test.

- 2026-08-15: A test that asserts CROSS-PROCESS behaviour must cross a real process boundary — an in-process proxy can pass while the defect is live. The obvious form of "the key persists" is two backend instances in one process resolving the same key; that would have passed throughout the corpus-key defect, because the non-persisting store keyring falls back to is process-GLOBAL, not per-instance. It proves the store is shared within a process and says nothing about a second one. The cheap real boundary for a Rust unit test is to re-execute the test binary: `std::env::current_exe()` + `--exact <test::path>`, with the parent passing state via env vars and the child writing its result to a temp sink the parent reads back. Pair it with a skip-clean guard where the dependency may be absent (CI has no credential store), and — the part that is easy to skip — VERIFY the child actually ran by running once with `--no-capture` and reading the nested test output, rather than trusting the green tick: a child that returns early still reports PASS. Generalizes to any claim about persistence, IPC, file locks, or singleton state across processes.

- 2026-08-15: Repairing a DEAD test fixture can expose a real product bug the test was written to catch but never reached — budget for a "test-only" fix not staying test-only. A fixture whose timestamps are ms-scale literals used as nanos sits in 1970, so any assertion behind a `now() - window` filter is unreachable and the test passes vacuously on the empty path. Fixing the fixture lets the test reach its real assertion for the FIRST time, and what it then reports is a finding, not a regression the repair introduced. When this happens, do NOT adjust the expectation to match current output — that encodes the defect as the contract and retires the guard permanently. Surface it: the correct resolution may be product code outside the chunk's scope (here the MCP sidecar never stamped the row id onto the decoded incident, so reports rendered id 0 and an incident listed itself as its own prior). The tell that a fixture is dead rather than merely old: its assertion is downstream of a relative-time or bounded-window filter that the fixture's absolute values can never satisfy.

- 2026-08-16: A timeout-bounded run that shells `cargo run` spends the budget COMPILING, and fails as a FALSE NEGATIVE rather than an obvious timeout — prebuild the binary, then invoke it by path. The danger is what that looks like downstream — the app boots fine, the log artifact exists, ticks emit, and the counter under test reads `0`, which is indistinguishable from the gate being broken. Measured this session: `seed_done rc=124` with `rows_ingested = 0` / `span_events_seen = 0`, and only the feed-precondition check (below) separated "the producer never ran" from "the feature is broken". Discipline: (a) `cargo build -p {crate} --example {name}` (or `--bin`) FIRST, outside the timed section, then run `./target/debug/examples/{name}.exe` by path inside it; (b) in any smoke asserting a downstream counter, assert the FEED advanced first — `rows_ingested > 0` — and print `INCONCLUSIVE` rather than a verdict when it did not; (c) treat a non-zero `rc` from the bounded producer as information, not noise: `124` means the budget expired, which is expected for a deliberately-bounded storm but is a red flag for a short seed. Generalizes to any harness step wrapping a cargo invocation in `timeout` — the compile is inside your budget unless you put it outside.

- 2026-08-17: To DISCHARGE (not merely assert) an acceptance criterion of the form "pinned so the losing behaviour fails the suite", run a MUTATION CHECK: temporarily neutralize the guard the new tests are supposed to be pinning — replace the predicate body with the pre-fix constant — re-run only the affected tests, confirm the new pins go RED, then restore. This is the positive-proof complement to the existing vacuity entries, which detect vacuity by inspection (assert the specific target rather than `!is_empty()`; audit a deterministic stub's payload completeness before grading on it); a mutation check instead proves the pin discriminates. Two payoffs beyond the criterion itself: it distinguishes a real regression pin from a test that would pass under both the old and new behaviour, and it tells you which PRE-EXISTING tests are insensitive to the change — those that stay green under the mutation never exercised the semantics you just changed, which is itself a finding about what the old suite covered. Cost is one build cycle of the touched crate. Verified when repairing stacktrace-normalization semantics: both new pins went red under the mutation while the pre-existing path-stripping test passed under both semantics, proving it had only ever exercised absolute paths and that the docs-vs-impl conflict was in the implementation alone. **[extended 2026-08-23]** For a CONDITIONAL property — "X happens ONLY when C" (a counter folds only on success; a cache writes only on miss; a retry fires only on a specific error) — the asymmetry is STRUCTURAL and predictable without waiting for the mutation to reveal it: the positive pin (X happens when C) passes under BOTH the correct implementation and the unconditional one, so it can never discriminate alone; only the negative pin (X does NOT happen when not-C) carries the guard. Write both, and treat the pair as one guard rather than two tests. The mutation check is what CONFIRMS which half is load-bearing: measured 2026-08-23 on the persisted-cells redaction fold, where moving the fold above the append turned the rejection pin RED (`left: 1, right: 0`) while the success pin stayed green — exactly as the pairing predicted. **[extended 2026-08-23] VERIFY THE MUTATION ACTUALLY APPLIED before reading the result — an unapplied mutation reports the INVERSE finding.** A mutation check reads green-on-mutation as "this pin does not discriminate", which is indistinguishable from "the mutation never landed": both print PASS. So an edit script that silently no-ops — a heredoc-quoted Python edit whose target line ends in a line-continuation backslash raises `SyntaxError` and changes nothing, while the following test run prints its usual PASS lines — manufactures a false negative about the pin, and the natural reading of that output is to weaken or delete a guard that was in fact sound. Two cheap defences: expect the RED and treat its ABSENCE as a failed mutation rather than a failed pin (the mutation's success criterion is that tests go red, so a green run is never the end of the check); and apply mutations with the anchored Edit tool, which errors loudly when its anchor does not match, rather than a shell-transported script. Verified when a mutation script failed to parse twice in one session and the second failure produced four PASS lines that read exactly like a non-discriminating read-path pin. **[extended 2026-08-29] A mutation check also grades the VERDICT, not just the pins — and a "half" can be non-discriminating because a DIFFERENT subsystem produces the same observable.** The 2026-08-23 facet above covers a half that cannot discriminate for a STRUCTURAL reason (the positive side of a conditional property). This is the independent-producer shape: an observable genuinely caused by the change is ALSO caused by an unrelated mechanism, so it moves identically in both arms and proves nothing. Measured at `2026-08-29-app-registry-reconciliation` while designing a live leg's two-half verdict: `item_count` was to be the second half ("the user-visible set shrank"), and it went **2 → 0 in BOTH arms** — because the finite storm's auto-resolve fires 120 s after the last re-emission and the observation window covered it, so the active set drained with or without the feature under test. Only `reconciled_count` (1 vs 0) and `declined_count` (0 vs 2) separated the worlds; the verdict was re-keyed onto those and both measured shapes pinned as a unit test. **The habit: for each half of a verdict, name what else in the system could produce that same signal in the window — and if anything can, the half is context, not evidence.** The plan had asserted the two halves were independent; only the mutation showed one was decorative. **[Extended 2026-10-04]** Never fire the mutation Edit and its test run in one parallel tool batch — the run cannot see the Edit's "string not found" error, so a formatter-reflowed anchor yields a green on the UNMUTATED tree; apply, grep-confirm the mutation is present, then run. Extended 2026-10-10: a mutation that removes one line of a fix does not restore the defect where the fix holds the property in two places — the pin stays green and reads as non-discriminating; put the base form of the block back instead.

- 2026-08-17: A PRE-EXISTING test can PIN THE DEFECT — and when a chunk deliberately flips that behaviour, the fix is to STRENGTHEN the assertion to the repaired truth, never to relax it to the new default. **This is the dual of the 2026-08-15 dead-fixture entry above, and the discriminator between them is whether the behaviour change was INTENDED by the chunk.** There: a repaired fixture reaches a real assertion for the first time and reports a genuine product defect → do NOT adjust the expectation (that encodes the defect as the contract). Here: the test asserts the OLD contract that the chunk exists to change → the assertion MUST move, but toward a stronger claim, not a weaker one. Two failure shapes to avoid when it moves: (a) **relaxing** — replacing the old expected value with whatever the new code now emits (e.g. asserting a field is empty because the fixture no longer populates it) retires the guard while looking green; (b) **going vacuous** — leaving the assertion's shape intact while the thing it varies stops reaching the assertion (a test that varied field X to prove "distinct X still coalesces" proves nothing once X no longer flows into the code under test). The repair for both is the same: re-point the test at whatever now carries the semantic, so it asserts the repaired contract with equal or greater force. Verified when a producer was repaired to write a threaded upstream hash instead of a model-authored string: one test asserted the incident's field equalled the model fixture's value (it pinned the defect, so it went red on the correct change and was re-pointed to assert the threaded value), and a second varied the model-authored field to prove a coalescing semantic (that field no longer reaches the incident, so it was re-pointed to vary the cue-borne one) — had either been relaxed instead, the suite would have stayed green while losing both guards.

- 2026-08-17: When two code paths must produce BYTE-IDENTICAL encodings for a comparison to work, share ONE function rather than two that are asserted to agree — and assert the exact VALUE or WIDTH, never merely the shape. A shape-only assertion (`chars().all(is_ascii_hexdigit)`, "is it a UUID", "is it base64") passes under BOTH the correct encoder and a wrong-width one, so it cannot discriminate. The hazard is sharpest when a correctly-named, adjacent helper encodes a DIFFERENT width for a different purpose: reaching for it is the obvious move, produces a value that can never match, and leaves every shape-only test green. Discipline: (a) put the encoder where both consumers already depend (a shared lower module), so agreement is structural rather than asserted; (b) in the pin, assert equality against the shared encoder's own output AND an explicit inequality against the look-alike helper — the inequality is what proves the test discriminates; (c) when a near-miss helper must survive alongside (a bounded-cardinality tracing prefix, a display truncation), say so in a comment at BOTH definitions naming the other. Verified where a 4-byte/8-char tracing prefix sat beside a 16-byte/32-char comparison encoding in the same crate; the width assertion plus the inequality is what makes the suite non-vacuous.

- 2026-08-17: A ZERO from a STATUS-FILTERED query is not evidence about the storage or the key — check the rows and the lifecycle clock before suspecting either. An active-only list surface (the MCP `query_incident_list` shape) returns `total: 0` on a fully healthy path once the auto-resolve window has elapsed, because the rows it filters for have legitimately left the queried status. That zero is indistinguishable at a glance from a workspace-key mismatch or a decryption failure, which are the expensive things to go chase. Discipline, in order: read the underlying rows directly (the corpus keeps `workspace` / `status` / `created` / `resolved` as plaintext columns beside the opaque payload, so a read-only sqlite open answers it without any key); compare the created-versus-resolved timestamps against the auto-resolve window; and confirm the absence of the diagnostics that a real key fault WOULD emit (`corpus.read.undecryptable`, a keychain-fallback warn) before concluding anything about custody. If the rows are present with a byte-matching workspace and no such diagnostic fired, the zero is the filter doing its job. Where an id-addressed sibling tool exists (`retrieve_telemetry_slice(incident_id)`), it bypasses the status filter entirely and is the faster probe. This is the same ambiguous-zero family as the fixture-id-collision and emit-site-authority entries above, with a third mechanism: a lifecycle transition, not a lost write and not a mis-attributed target.

- 2026-08-17: A guard that ITERATES a collection proves nothing when the collection is empty — pair every content guard with a discriminating presence guard, or it guards nothing on its own. A `for x in &collection { assert!(property(x)) }` test passes vacuously at length zero: the loop body never runs, so the assertion inside it is never evaluated, and the test reports green for exactly the regression it was written to catch (the collection emptying out). Shape-only assertions have the same defect from a different direction — asserting a value "looks like hex" cannot separate a correct encoding from a wrong-width one. So a content property and a presence/value property are two different guards and both are needed: assert the exact expected values (or at minimum a non-zero count) in one test, and the per-element property in another. The cheap way to know which of your guards actually discriminate is a MUTATION CHECK — neutralize the thing under guard, confirm the intended pins go red, restore. Verified when a scrubber-survival pin written in the same chunk as its subject passed vacuously under the mutation while the value pin beside it went red; the pair was sound, the content pin alone would not have been.

- 2026-08-22: MAKE "MEASURE FIRST" MECHANICAL, NOT PROCEDURAL — write the POST-FIX assertion first and run it BEFORE the fix; its failure output IS the measurement. A chunk asked to prove a defect exists before repairing it usually does so with a throwaway probe, then writes the real test afterwards — which leaves the measurement unrecorded and the test unproven as a discriminator. Inverting the order gets both from one artifact: the committed test runs RED against unfixed code (that run is the evidence, quotable in the report), then GREEN after, so red→green on the real path replaces "I checked, it was broken." It also forecloses the worst outcome — a test written after the fix that would have passed before it. And it makes premise-correction free: if the assertion passes COLD, the defect does not exist, the chunk stops and reports that instead of reshaping itself to preserve the finding. Verified at 2026-08-22-pii-scrubber-recall: the bare-credential canary test failed on both routes before the catalog arm landed (stored value equal to the canary verbatim, no redaction marker) and passed after, on the real OTLP→DuckDB path rather than a regex assertion.

- 2026-08-22: A NEW COUNTER READING ZERO PROVES THE PLUMBING, NOT THE BEHAVIOUR — drive a real trigger before believing it. The vacuity family above covers empty collections (2026-08-17) and stub payloads (2026-08-16); this is the counter-shaped sibling. A freshly-added aggregate field that appears in the log with value `0` demonstrates only that the emit site and the allowlist leaf resolve — the fold arithmetic behind it is completely unexercised, and `0` is exactly what a permanently-broken increment would also print. Worse, the healthy case and the dead case are indistinguishable at a glance, so the field reads as "verified present" in a report while guarding nothing. Discipline: after observing the field exists, drive a real instance of the thing it counts and assert it ADVANCES (the delta is the proof, not the presence); where the standard seed carries no such instance, construct one deliberately rather than accepting the zero. Verified at 2026-08-22-pii-scrubber-recall: `redactions_applied` rode `buffer.tick` unredacted at `0` under the demo injector (which emits no credentials) and only a hand-encoded bare-credential canary moved it 0 → 1, which is what actually proved the counter. **[extended 2026-08-26] The PLANNED driver can be structurally incapable of moving the counter — check the evaluator's math before spending the run, not after.** A chunk plan's smoke may name a load profile that cannot produce the condition under test: here `inject_demo --sustained --minutes=15` holds a CONSTANT error rate, and the cue evaluator's magnitude is a short/long EWMA RATIO, so the long window converges on the short one and the ratio falls back under its 3.0 gate — no cue re-fires, and the bound's counter reads 0 for fifteen minutes while everything looks green. Measured live in the same run that proved it: Phase A ticks under sustained load carried `cues_emitted 0 / cues_latched 0`; only stopping the producer (so every service crossed its silence threshold) drove 887 refusals. **Two habits follow.** (a) Before a long smoke, read the code that DECIDES the condition and name the lever that makes it recur — often an env-gated bound (`ANDROMEDA_PULSE_BASELINE_BOOTSTRAP_SECONDS=60` was the lever here; the 3600s default cannot elapse inside any smoke). (b) Treat a zero from the planned form as INCONCLUSIVE until the driver itself is shown capable — a plan is a proposal about the verification, never proof that the verification bites.

- 2026-08-24: PROBE INVISIBLY-RENDERING CONSTANTS BY CODEPOINT, NEVER BY PRINTED APPEARANCE — a diagnostic sibling of the 2026-06-05 tail-masked-exit-code entry (both are output-appearance lying about program state). `console.log`/`JSON.stringify` of a string whose value is a Private Use Area codepoint (wdio's `Key.Shift` = ``, `Key.Escape` = `` — the W3C key sentinels) renders as an EMPTY string in the terminal, which reads exactly like a broken/empty constant. Measured at `2026-08-23-headful-leg-extension`: the "Key constants are empty" reading briefly stood as the root cause for three failing stages and would have driven a wrong fix; a codepoint-level probe (`[...v].map(c=>c.codePointAt(0).toString(16))`) disproved it in one call and the real cause was elsewhere. Rule: before concluding any constant/sentinel is empty or wrong from its printed form, print its `length` and codepoints; a zero-looking value with `length >= 1` is a rendering artifact, not a value.

- 2026-08-25: BLOCK-BUFFERED STDOUT MAKES A HANG LOOK LIKE A SLOW RUN — the third member of the output-appearance-lies family (2026-06-05 tail-masked exit code · 2026-08-24 PUA codepoints), and the most expensive so far. Node (and most runtimes) LINE-buffer stdout to a TTY but BLOCK-buffer it to a file or pipe, so a redirected long-running driver's visible output lags reality by up to a buffer, and a process killed at a timeout never flushes the tail. The trap is not the missing output — it is the INFERENCE it invites: two runs killed at different ceilings stop at the SAME visible stage (both show one buffer's worth), which reads as compelling evidence of a hang AT that stage and is in fact evidence of nothing about location. Measured at `2026-08-24-headful-mechanics-probe-race-disposition`: that reading drove three ceiling raises (420 → 660 → 1200s) before a run went long enough to flush the real signature — a dead WebDriver session several stages later. **Rules: (a) never infer a hang LOCATION from where redirected output stops; (b) when you must locate one, make the run long enough to flush, or have the harness write a per-stage artifact it fsyncs (this leg's `webview-drive-stages.json` exists for exactly that and was the reliable record throughout); (c) treat "two runs stopped identically" as a buffering signature first and a determinism signal second.** Corollary: a raised timeout that does not change the outcome is disconfirming evidence for the slow-run hypothesis — stop raising it.

- 2026-08-26: AN ENFORCEMENT GUARD HAS TWO ARMS AND BOTH NEED LIVE PROOF — the POSITIVE arm is the does-not-brick-the-host proof, and it is the one that gets left implied. A guard chunk naturally produces vivid negative evidence: the rejection fires, the category is right, the log is clean. That evidence proves the guard BITES; it says nothing about whether a legitimate configuration still works, and unit tests covering the accept path are not a substitute, because the thing at risk is the wiring and the environment, not the predicate. The asymmetry is practical: a too-strict guard passes every negative test, ships, and disables the feature for everyone — which is exactly the failure a smoke leg would have caught in seconds. Discipline: for any chunk that adds an enforcement boundary, enumerate the arms before writing the smoke plan (reject-the-bad · accept-the-good · and the not-configured default if one exists) and give each its own leg with its own fresh data dir; when an arm genuinely cannot run live, state it as unit-only IN THE REPORT rather than letting the passing negative legs imply full coverage. Verified at `2026-08-26-l4-runtime-security-residuals`, on an operator directive: the plan's two legs proved rejection and the unconfined default, while "a legitimate out-of-tree model still loads when the declared root contains it" was unit-proven only; the added third leg produced the enforced posture record with zero rejections and cost one boot. Pairs with the 2026-08-22 measure-first entry (that one sequences the RED before the fix; this one insists the GREEN side is a leg, not an inference).

- 2026-08-28: A WAIT/POLL PREDICATE KEYED ON A REDACTED OBSERVABLE CAN NEVER FIRE — and its silence reads as a measurement. The vacuity family already covers an empty collection (2026-08-17) and a zero counter (2026-08-22); this is the harness-side member and its mechanism is the ALLOWLIST, not the data. A smoke leg that polls the log for a field on a target with no exact leaf matches nothing whatever the truth is, because the field renders `"<redacted>"` — so the loop runs to its ceiling and the natural reading of that silence is "the condition never occurred", which is a false claim about the system rather than about the check. Two habits: before keying any wait, assertion, or `grep`-based gate on a self-observation FIELD, confirm that field's target has its own exact allowlist leaf (a target falling back to a bare prefix key, or to nothing, redacts silently); and treat a poll that runs its full ceiling as INCONCLUSIVE until the field is shown to render, never as a negative result. Measured at `2026-08-27-incident-persist-vs-resolve-write-race`: a GREEN-leg loop polled `resolved_count` on `triage.incident.auto_resolve.tick` — a target the chunk's own research had recorded as resolving to NO entry — and ran its full 300s; the resolutions had in fact happened, proven from `item_count` and a corpus read-back. Pairs with the 2026-08-15 emit-site-is-the-authority rule: that one governs what a leaf must CONTAIN, this one governs what you may CONCLUDE from a field you have not confirmed renders.

- 2026-08-28: REPRODUCE A TWO-WRITER RACE WITH AN INTERLEAVING TEST DOUBLE, NOT WITH TIMING. When a defect needs writer B to land inside writer A's critical section, the reproduction looks like it needs real concurrency — which collides head-on with the §11 `sleep` ban and the zero-flakiness budget. It usually does not. If A is a synchronous function over injected `&dyn` dependencies and B is pure with respect to time (takes its instant as an argument), wrap A's dependency in a test double whose first call invokes B and then delegates to the real implementation: B now lands inside A's write span deterministically, with no clock, no interval, and no `sleep`. Prefer this over `tokio::time::pause` when the race is between two SYNCHRONOUS writers rather than two timers — pausing the clock does not interleave them, and driving the real intervals reintroduces the flake. Verified at `2026-08-27-incident-persist-vs-resolve-write-race`, where the persist cycle and the auto-resolve observer have exactly that shape; the resulting pin reddened under a mutation of the production guard while the accept-arm pins correctly stayed green in both worlds.

- 2026-08-28: WHAT A MEASURE-FIRST **RED LEG PRODUCES DEPENDS ON THE DEFECT'S SHAPE** — and one of the two shapes emits nothing at all, which turns the clean-log assertion into a vacuous pass. A REJECT-shaped defect (a write refused, a batch failed, a guard firing) emits the ERROR it is measuring, which is why the 2026-08-23 rule scopes the 0-ERROR assertion to the GREEN leg only. A **BLOCK-shaped** defect emits nothing — nothing returns, so nothing reports — so a RED leg over it carries **0 `ERROR` and 0 `app.panic.fatal`** and reads, line for line, like a perfectly healthy run. Asserting "0 ERROR" there passes for entirely the wrong reason, exactly like the guard-that-iterates-an-empty-collection and the counter-reading-zero above. For a block-shaped defect the evidence of record is **absence of progress**: a frozen progress counter, consecutive zero-delta heartbeat ticks, and whatever transition WARN the progress classifier emits — never an ERROR. **Decide which shape you are measuring BEFORE choosing the leg's evidence**, and if a RED leg comes back with a clean log, that is a question to answer rather than a result to record. Measured at `2026-08-28-ingest-consumer-initiating-freeze`: a RED leg reproduced a 450 s consumer stall — 24k+ accepted spans never persisted — with 0 ERROR and 0 panics throughout, falsifying test-plan §3's then-standing claim that a RED leg "MUST produce the ERROR it is measuring" (§3 amended the same wrap).

- 2026-08-29: CARGO DEFAULTS AN AUTO-DISCOVERED `[[example]]` TARGET TO `test = false` — so `#[cfg(test)] mod tests` inside an example compiles, passes under `cargo test --example X`, and is collected ZERO times by `cargo nextest run --workspace`. This is the THIRD member of the dead-test family in this file, after pulse-app's `[lib] test = false` (2026-05-20: source-level `mod tests` never runs) and its clippy corollary (2026-06-04: `--all-targets` still COMPILES them, so they must stay compile-clean). The example variant is the most deceptive of the three because the tests genuinely RUN — just never in the gate: a targeted `cargo test --example` prints a confident green while the workspace suite has never seen them, so a chunk can report "8 new pins" over a gate that collected none of them. **The fix is a manifest declaration** — an explicit `[[example]] name = "…" path = "…" test = true` in the crate's `Cargo.toml`; auto-discovery cannot express it. **The detection is arithmetic, and it is the part worth internalizing: check that the workspace test count moved by the amount you added.** Measured 2026-08-28 at `2026-08-28-duplicate-span-replay-fails-loudly`: 12 tests added (1 appender + 8 injector + 3 xtask) and the suite moved 2044 → 2048, a delta of +4; every gate was green in both worlds and nothing but the count discrepancy pointed at the 8 uncollected tests. Verify with `cargo nextest list --workspace --profile ci | grep -c <target>` before believing a test landed in the gate — and treat a delta that does not match the count you wrote as a finding, not a rounding detail. Extended 2026-10-05: an example file is a crate ROOT, so its `mod x;` resolves to `examples/x.rs` — a path Cargo auto-discovers as a NEW example — never to `examples/{example}/x.rs`; wire a module beside an example with `#[path = "{example}/x.rs"]`.

- 2026-08-29: EXTENSION to the 2026-06-05 `| tail`-masks-the-exit-code entry (background commands, then wait predicates) — the SAME masking bites in the plainest FOREGROUND shape: `some-gate 2>&1 | tail -3; echo "exit=$?"` reports `tail`'s exit code, not the gate's, so a failing gate prints `exit=0`. Measured 2026-08-28 running `cargo deny check bans licenses sources | tail -3; echo exit=$?`: the pipeline printed `exit=0` while the gate's own text said `bans FAILED` — the TEXT was the real signal and the number was noise. The recovery is the same discipline in a third setting: redirect to a file and read `$?` from the unpiped command (`cmd > /tmp/out.txt 2>&1; echo "REAL EXIT=$?"`), then inspect the file. Corollary worth stating because it nearly inverted the reading here: when a tool prints its own verdict, prefer the tool's words over a captured `$?` you did not isolate.

- 2026-08-30: A SUITE-HEALTH PROBE IN A MULTI-CONFIG PLAYWRIGHT REPO MUST NAME THE CONFIG — this repo carries a deliberately-inert default `playwright.config.ts` (0 tests) beside the real `playwright-a11y.config.ts` (37 tests / 16 files), so a bare `npx playwright test --list` reports "Total: 0 tests in 0 files" with exit 1: a reading indistinguishable from the list-time-import silent-death mode the probe exists to catch (a11y-plan §3), except that here the SUITE IS FINE and the probe inspected the wrong subject. Measured live at `2026-08-30-npm-advisory-coverage` — the a11y chain had just run 37/37 green, which is what exposed the 0 as probe misdirection rather than suite death. The probe form is `npx playwright test --config=playwright-a11y.config.ts --list`; a 0-count from the bare form is a question about the invocation, never a verdict about the suite. The vacuity-family facet worth keeping: a health check aimed at the wrong subject fails exactly like the defect it guards against.

- 2026-08-30: THE BUNDLED `ARGS_MAP` DECIDES A TAURPC METHOD'S RUNTIME EXISTENCE — the RUNTIME facet of the bindings-regen family (2026-05-13 / 2026-05-17 / 2026-08-15 here; 2026-06-12 in `rules/security.md`, which govern the COMMIT hygiene). The taurpc webview proxy resolves methods against the `ARGS_MAP` constant generated into `pulse-app/ui/src/bindings/index.ts` and BUNDLED into `ui/dist` at `npm run build` — the backend advertising the procedure is irrelevant to the lookup. So a procedure and its first caller added in the SAME chunk are runtime-invisible until regen → `npm run build` → re-embed, in that order, BEFORE any live leg that exercises the caller; and a fire-and-forget caller (`.catch(() => {})`, the sanctioned reporter shape) makes the miss SILENT — no error, no record, every committed test green — so the wire assert is the only discriminator. Measured at `2026-08-30-acl-rejection-logging`: the first revoked-arm leg read 0 `ui.ipc.rejection` records because the dist predated the regen (its single `record_ipc_rejection` string was the caller's own property access, not the map entry — a 1-vs-2 occurrence grep on the minified bundle separates the two); regen → dist → release re-embed produced exactly the expected record. The gate-side regen-LAST ordering (playbook 2026-08-22) is COMPATIBLE, not contradicted: release builds and release-binary runs never emit bindings, so a mid-session regen survives to the staged gate untouched — regen-before-live-leg and regen-before-staging are the same regen when sequenced regen → dist → release → legs → stage.

- 2026-09-29: `cargo llvm-cov`'s FUNCTION % COUNTS EACH COMPILED COPY OF A FUNCTION — a library function tested in its own crate still reads UNCOVERED in every other test binary that links a copy of it (generic instantiations and per-binary copies each get a row), so a workspace function % can sit below its gate while every function has a test. Before chasing a function-coverage shortfall with new tests, check whether the uncovered rows are copies of already-tested functions; the scope of the measure (which binaries' copies count) moves the number as much as the tests do.

- 2026-09-30: A TEST INPUT ECHOED INTO A COMMITTED EVIDENCE LOG CAN TRIP THE RUN-DIR HYGIENE CHECK. Nextest output carries each failing case's panic message, and that message quotes the test's input verbatim. So a RED-before or mutation-check log saved under a chunk's `evidence/` holds every literal a failing case asserted on. A path-shaped fixture (a Windows drive-letter path written to exercise a path form) then reads as a host path to the hygiene gate's drive-path predicate, which refuses the file although nothing on the host leaked. Replace the echoed literal in the committed log with a labelled placeholder, leaving the source literal as it is. Extended 2026-10-04: a saved `gate.py run` stdout capture no longer trips it on the tool's own header lines — gate v1.10 prints the repo root as `.`, its log dir as `$TMPDIR/andromeda-gate` and the home as `~` [corrected 2026-10-05: before v1.10 those `root` / `logs` lines printed the absolute paths and needed placeholdering]; a host path the plan's own text holds (`/tmp/x`, a drive path) still prints as written and still needs it. Extended 2026-10-04: a hand-written evidence transcript trips the same check — a pasted `ls` line naming a file under the system temp dir reads as a host path, so write it with a labelled `{tmp}` placeholder, and re-run hygiene after any evidence edit that follows its first read.

- 2026-09-30: SWEEP HAZARD — when a chunk changes a VALUE inside a data artifact (a manifest field, a literal in a generated-file template), find the tests that pin it by grepping the test trees for the OLD VALUE's literal (`grep -rn '<old literal>' crates pulse-app/tests xtask`), not for the artifact's file name: a test that reads a workflow file and asserts a substring never names the manifest the chunk edited, and a substring pin stays green on a superstring but reds the moment the value's closing delimiter moves (`"MIT"` → `"MIT|Apache-2.0"`). **[Extended 2026-10-04]** Grep the BARE value with a word boundary (`v2\.3\b`), never its quoted form: a test can embed the value unquoted inside a longer string (`"prompt_version=v2.3"`), which a `'"v2\.3"'` sweep never matches.

(os error 5)`. The bash tool's timeout reaps the spawning shell + `head -60` filter pipe but does NOT cascade-kill the child Tauri process. **Diagnostic recipe:** `tasklist | grep -iE "pulse|tauri"` after suspicious bash timeout to surface the orphan PID. **Recovery:** `Stop-Process -Id <PID> -Force` via PowerShell (`taskkill /F /PID <N>` from git bash misinterprets `/F` as a Unix path; use cmd.exe or PowerShell). Mass-killing (`taskkill /F /IM cargo.exe /T`) is correctly blocked by Claude Code's auto-mode classifier because it affects shared dev environment; kill-by-specific-PID is the safe path. **Prevention for future Phase 2b smoke runs on Windows:** prefer `cargo build -p pulse-app` (no Tauri runtime spawn) + integration-test runtime smoke (e.g., `pulse-app::e2e_p1_otlp_grpc_to_traces_query` exercises boot+ingest+query roundtrip in ~2s) as a lightweight runtime-smoke alternative for non-UI chunks. The dangerous part is not the failure but its SHAPE when the probe is written `tasklist /FI … || echo "not running"`: a zero-is-healthy `||` fallback fires on the COMMAND ERROR and prints a conclusion indistinguishable from a genuine negative result, so a liveness/absence check reports "not running" without ever having looked. Write such probes with PowerShell (`Get-Process -Id N -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue`) whose exit semantics survive the shell, and never let a `||` branch be the only thing that produces the answer — the branch must be reachable ONLY by the probe genuinely succeeding-and-finding-nothing.
